extracted.intended_audience: graduate students / advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (scheme-theoretic algebraic geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Solving and understanding textbook-level exercises and statements in scheme-theoretic algebraic geometry (definitions, theorems, and sample computations) as presented in Ravi Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: K3 surface
rubrics_metrics.description: A K3 surface over a field k is a proper smooth geometrically connected Calabi–Yau surface X over k such that H^1(X, O_X) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify K3 surfaces; exercise (21.5.I) asks to prove that the dimension 2 smooth Calabi–Yau complete intersections of Exercise 21.5.H(c) are all K3 surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kodaira Vanishing Theorem (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose k is a field of characteristic 0, and X is a smooth projective k-variety. Then for any ample invertible sheaf L, H^i(X, K_X ⊗ L) = 0 for i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The characteristic 0 restriction is necessary (Raynaud gave counterexamples in positive characteristic). Original proof uses complex-analytic methods and Serre's GAGA; more algebraic approaches (Lefschetz principle reductions, DeI/Il) are mentioned. There are exercises to prove Kodaira vanishing for dim X = 1 and for P^n_k which do not require char 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge numbers and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The invariant h^{i,j}(X) := dim H^j(X, Ω^i_{X/k}) is called the Hodge number h_{i,j}(X). By Exercise 21.5.A, h_{i,0} are birational invariants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming Miracle 18.5.2 (canonical bundle is Serre-dualizing), Serre duality gives symmetry h_{p,q} = h_{n-p,n-q}. Over k = C there is the Hodge decomposition H^m(X,C) = ⊕_{i+j=m} H^j(X,Ω^i_{X/C}) and complex conjugation gives h_{i,j} = h_{j,i}. Examples and Hodge diamonds for curves, surfaces, and P^n are provided; exercises compute these explicitly (21.5.M, 21.5.N, 21.5.O).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge numbers of projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: For P^n_k, h_{p,q}(P^n_k) = 0 except h_{p,p} = 1 for 0 ≤ p ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use the Euler exact sequence (Theorem 21.4.6) and apply Exercise 13.5.F; this shows the Hodge diamond for P^n has 1's down the middle axis and 0 elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge diamond examples and invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: for an irreducible smooth projective complex surface the Hodge diamond has symmetries coming from Serre duality and complex conjugation; for a genus g curve the Hodge diamond is [g; 1 1; g], and h_{1,1} equals the Picard number ρ in these cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 21.5.N and O guide computation of these diamonds and note where h_{1,1} is or isn't a birational invariant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimal automorphisms and deformations (cohomological description)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a variety, H^0(X, T_X) parametrizes infinitesimal automorphisms of X, and H^1(X, T_X) parametrizes infinitesimal deformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for X = P^1, T_{P^1} ≅ O(2) so h^0(P^1, T_{P^1}) = 3, matching the dimension of Aut(P^1). Exercises compute h^i(C, T_C) for curves of genus g (21.5.R) with expected dimensions 0,1,3g-3 for g = 0,1,>1 respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: formally unramified and unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism π: X → Y, the support of Ω_π = Ω_{X/Y} is the ramification locus. If Ω_π = 0, π is formally unramified; if additionally π is locally of finite type, then π is unramified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: some sources use 'locally of finite presentation' instead of 'locally of finite type'. This gives a scheme-theoretic notion of ramification; many exercises explore examples and characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples of unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally closed embeddings are unramified; Spec S^{-1}B → Spec B for multiplicative S is formally unramified; finite separable field extension maps are unramified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.6.A lists these standard examples; they are used to build intuition and test definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of unramified morphisms by fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: (21.6.D) π is unramified iff for each q ∈ Y, π^{-1}(q) is (scheme-theoretically) a disjoint union of Spec K where K is a finite separable extension of κ(q); equivalently for each geometric point q, π^{-1}(q) is a disjoint union of copies of q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fiberwise description gives a practical test for unramifiedness in many settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior: stability and local openness of unramifiedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Unramified morphisms are preserved by composition (if π and ρ are unramified then ρ◦π is unramified). The locus in X where π is unramified is open (Exercise 21.6.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are routine but important properties used in geometric arguments and checking local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization via diagonal: unramified iff diagonal is open embedding (Noetherian case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y locally finite type of locally Noetherian schemes, π is unramified iff the diagonal δ_π: X → X ×_Y X is an open embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.6.F gives the proof and a hint to remove the Noetherian hypothesis by using finite presentation; this is a key intrinsic characterization of unramified morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic remark: different and discriminant measure ramification
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is the ring of integers in a number field, the different ideal of B is the annihilator of Ω_{B/ Z}; the discriminant ideal corresponds to the pushforward of the different. These ideals are ring-theoretic versions of the ramification locus and discriminant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties the geometric notion of ramification to classical arithmetic invariants; the text notes the connection but does not use it further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: separable (finite / generically finite) morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite morphism between integral schemes X → Y is separable if it is dominant and the induced extension of function fields K(X)/K(Y) is separable. Generically finite is generically separable if the induced extension of function fields is separable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: finite morphisms of integral schemes are automatically separable in characteristic 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative cotangent exactness for generically separable maps (21.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a generically separable morphism of irreducible smooth varieties of the same dimension n, then the relative cotangent sequence is exact on the left: 0 → π^*Ω_{Y/k} → Ω_{X/k} → Ω_{X/Y} → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This injectivity is checked at the generic point using separability. The statement underlies the interpretation of the ramification locus as where φ fails to be an isomorphism and motivates the ramification divisor construction. Examples of non-separable maps (char p) show failure and presence of vertical tangent vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramification locus and ramification divisor (purity and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For generically separable π between smooth varieties of equal dimension, the ramification locus is pure codimension 1 and can be interpreted as the vanishing of the determinant of the Jacobian matrix; hence it defines an effective divisor called the ramification divisor. The branch locus downstairs is similarly codimension 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.A walks through interpreting φ as an n×n Jacobian and identifying the ramification/branch divisors; in dimension 1 (curves) ramification points are finite and the local ramification order matches the vanishing order of differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tame vs wild ramification and local computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Local model: if uniformizers satisfy t = u s^n (u unit), then dt has vanishing order at least n−1 and exactly n−1 if n not divisible by characteristic (tame); otherwise wild ramification occurs. The degree of Ω_{X/Y} at a point equals the ramification order at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.B asks to show the degree of Ω_{X/Y} at p equals the ramification order; this distinguishes tame/wild phenomena and is used to compute contributions to the ramification divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation: ramification multiplicity counts missing preimages (21.7.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite separable morphism π : X → Y over algebraically closed k and tame ramification above q, the degree of the branch divisor at q equals deg π − |π^{-1}(q)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus multiplicity of branch divisor measures how the number of geometric preimages falls short of the degree; illustrated in Figure 21.4 and Exercise 21.7.C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Hurwitz formula (21.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X → Y is a finite separable morphism of projective regular curves of pure degree n. Let R be the ramification divisor. Then 2g(X) − 2 = n(2g(Y) − 2) + deg R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.D suggests proving this by applying degree-additivity to the exact sequence (21.7.2.1). The formula underlies many consequences: parity of deg R, impossibility of certain maps between curves of given genera, fundamental-group consequences (P^1 simply connected), and Luroth's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: parity and constraints from Riemann–Hurwitz
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of the ramification divisor R is always even; for example, there is no nonconstant map from a genus 2 curve to a genus 3 curve (Exercise 21.7.E). The only connected unbranched finite separable cover of P^1_k (k algebraically closed) is the isomorphism (Example 21.7.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Riemann–Hurwitz with R = 0 to constrain degrees and genera; Exercises 21.7.E–G expand these corollaries and note characteristic p exceptions (Artin–Schreier covers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lüroth's theorem (geometric consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g(X) = 0 for a finite map π: X → Y of curves (with prior hypotheses), then g(Y) = 0; equivalently, subfields of k(x) containing k are of the form k(y) with y = f(x) ∈ k(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivable from Riemann–Hurwitz; the text notes the hypotheses char k = 0 and k algebraically closed are not necessary for the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds on automorphism groups of curves (Hurwitz bound sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an irreducible smooth projective curve C of genus g ≥ 2 over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, a finite automorphism group G satisfies |G| ≤ 84(g − 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 21.7.K–M guide construction: form quotient C' with morphism of degree |G|, analyze branch points and ramification orders, and minimize certain expressions (21.7.8.1) to obtain the 84(g−1) bound. Remarks note larger automorphism groups can occur in positive characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up: universal property definition
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed subscheme X ↪ Y (finite type quasi-coherent ideal), the blow-up Bl_X Y is a Cartesian diagram EXY → X, Bl_X Y → Y such that EXY (the scheme-theoretic pullback of X) is an effective Cartier divisor on Bl_X Y, and any other Cartesian diagram with D an effective Cartier divisor factors uniquely through it. EXY is the exceptional divisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universal property characterizes the blow-up uniquely up to unique isomorphism. Observations: blow-up is an isomorphism away from X; if X is empty Bl_X Y = Y; if X is an effective Cartier divisor the blow-up is the identity; if X = Y the blow-up is empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local nature and existence for locally principal centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up is local on Y: if U ⊂ Y is open then Bl_{X∩U} U ≅ β^{-1}(U). For X locally cut out by one equation (locally principal closed subscheme), the blow-up exists and can be described affinely (Spec A/I → Spec A with I = ker(A → A_t) where t cuts out X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 22.2.D–F guide the affine construction: show φ(t) not zerodivisor in A/I, that Spec A/I → Spec A is the blow-up diagram, and that Spec A/I is the scheme-theoretic closure of D(t) in Spec A (geometric interpretation: shaving off fuzz supported in V(t)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and consequences of blowing up
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper transform (strict transform) of Z is β^{-1}(Z − X) closure; the total transform β^{-1}Z is the scheme-theoretic pullback; blow-up preserves reducedness and irreducibility (if X doesn't contain the generic point); the exceptional divisor is an effective Cartier divisor; the blow-up morphism is projective (deduced later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blow-up closure lemma (22.2.6) states that proper transform of Z is naturally isomorphic to Bl_Z (X ∩ Z) in relevant situations. The motivating examples (blowing up origin in A^2, An, or an m-plane) show how blow-up separates directions and can desingularize certain singularities (strict transform).
